label: Person
name: Perdiccas III of Macedon
summary:
Perdiccas III of Macedon (reigned 365–360 BCE) was king of the Argead dynasty and the elder brother of Philip II, whose death in battle transformed Macedonian history and inadvertently enabled the rise of Alexander the Great.

Coming to power after his brother Alexander II's assassination (365 BCE), Perdiccas faced a kingdom beset by rivals and constant Illyrian pressure on Macedonia's western frontier. He ruled for five years, managing the complex regional politics of northern Greece while struggling to maintain the loyalty of the Macedonian nobility. His younger brother Philip served in his court after returning from Theban exile.

His reign ended catastrophically in 360 BCE when he led the Macedonian army against the Illyrian king Bardylis at the Battle of the Lyncestian plain and was killed along with approximately 4,000 soldiers — more than a third of Macedonia's entire military strength. The disaster left his infant son Amyntas IV as nominal heir. Philip II, then approximately 23 years old, stepped in as regent and seized the throne, rebuilt the Macedonian army with the revolutionary sarissa-equipped phalanx, and crushed Bardylis at the Battle of Erigon Valley in 358 BCE. Perdiccas III's catastrophic defeat thus became, paradoxically, the catalyst that transformed Macedonia from a vulnerable buffer state into the dominant power of the Greek world.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Perdiccas III's reign was marked by power struggles and the eventual partitioning of Macedonia, setting a turning point in the Hellenistic period.

causes: Alexander II of Macedon's assassination (365 BCE) created a succession crisis that Perdiccas had to resolve by force
Illyrian king Bardylis's sustained military pressure on Macedonia's western frontier drew Perdiccas into a decisive confrontation
Macedonian nobility's factional competition required the king to demonstrate military strength to maintain authority
effects: Death of 4,000 Macedonian soldiers (c. 360 BCE) — the catastrophic defeat that stripped Macedonia of its military capacity
Philip II's seizure of the regency and then the throne, enabled by Perdiccas's death and infant heir Amyntas IV
Philip II's military reforms (358 BCE) — the sarissa phalanx, cavalry arm, and siege engineering — born from the humiliation of Perdiccas's defeat
Macedonian hegemony over Greece (346–338 BCE) — ultimately flowing from Philip's response to the crisis Perdiccas created
Alexander the Great's conquests (334–323 BCE) — made possible by the military machine Philip built after inheriting Perdiccas's disaster

relationships.context: Perdiccas succeeded his brother as king of Macedonia.
The two generals vied for control over Macedonian territory.
The conflicts surrounding Perdiccas' reign had significant regional implications.
As one of the Diadochi, Ptolemy eventually eclipsed Perdiccas' ambitions.
Perdiccas III ruled from Pella, the royal capital of Macedonia.
Perdiccas' reign had significant regional implications for Macedonia and its neighboring territories.
The influence of Perdiccas' reign extended to the Hellenistic city of Alexandria.
The dynamics of Perdiccas' reign were also influenced by the larger European context.
